subject: Civil Engineering
title: Soil Liquefaction: When Ground Turns Liquid
description: Learn Soil Liquefaction: When Ground Turns Liquid in one minute.

hook.text: In the 1964 Niigata earthquake, apartment buildings tipped over like dominoes — into mud.

buildup.text: Earthquake shaking compresses loose, saturated sand. Water pressure spikes instantly.

discovery.text: When pore water pressure equals the soil's weight, grains float — liquefaction.

twist.text: Solid ground becomes quicksand in seconds. Heavy structures sink; light ones float up.

climax.text: Engineers prevent liquefaction by densifying soil or installing drainage before building.

punchline.text: Earthquakes don't just shake — they melt the ground.

quiz.question: What causes soil liquefaction during an earthquake?
options: Heat from friction melts the soil particles
Pore water pressure rises until grains lose contact and float
Chemical reactions dissolve the bonds between soil grains

details.summary: Soil liquefaction occurs during earthquake shaking when pore water pressure in loose saturated sand rises to equal the confining soil pressure, reducing effective stress to zero.
details.whyItMatters: Liquefaction has caused billions of dollars in damage in modern earthquakes, including Christchurch 2011, where it destroyed thousands of buildings across entire suburbs built on liquefiable alluvial deposits.
takeaways: Pore pressure rise during shaking reduces effective stress to zero in loose saturated sand
Sand boils erupt at the surface as pressurized water and sand escape upward
Ground improvement through densification is the primary mitigation strategy

faq.question: What are sand boils and what do they indicate?
faq.answer: Sand boils are cone-shaped deposits of sand that erupt at the ground surface during or after an earthquake. They form when liquefied soil below is squeezed by overlying non-liquefied layers, forcing a mixture of water and sand upward through cracks.

faq.question: How is liquefaction potential evaluated at a construction site?
faq.answer: Engineers compare the cyclic stress ratio generated by the design earthquake with the cyclic resistance ratio of the soil from Standard Penetration Tests, Cone Penetration Tests, or shear wave velocity measurements.
